Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices weighed on consumption and net exports.
A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter.
Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, but net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth.
Energy subsidies for households had reportedly expired in September, exposing consumers to higher energy prices brought about by the Iran war.
The GDP data could complicate Japan's policy normalization path, though there's still a 75.6% chance of the Bank of Japan raising rates by 25 basis points in December, according to LSEG.
"Today's GDP data is hardly a green light for the BOJ to hike in December," according to Krishna Bhimavarapu, APAC economist at State Street Investment Management.

An evacuation order that forced hundreds of people from their homes near an industrial site in central Illinois was lifted Saturday after law enforcement agencies completed a search of the area, authorities said.
A bomb was discovered Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. Police said the device had been “rendered safe,” but authorities ordered residents within a 1-mile radius to evacuate while the surrounding area was searched.
State, federal and local law enforcement conducted an extensive search at the facility and “they have found no other items of concern,” the Peoria Police Department said on its Facebook account on Saturday. “Residents are now free to return to their homes in the area that was affected,” the police said, adding that all roads will be opened and the investigation will continue.
FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.
“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” he said.
No arrests have been made at this time, and no injuries have been reported.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is “a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us.”
It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don’t result in a credible threat, even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.
“We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said. “We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe.”
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.

The Florida Surplus Lines Service Office announced a $12 million gift to Florida State University’s risk management and insurance program, a grant that should enable deeper research into Florida’s ever-evolving insurance landscape.
It’s by far the largest grant yet for FSLSO, which has donated $2.5 million to universities in the state since the stamping office began operations 28 years ago.
The endowment, which leaders with FSU’s Herbert Wertheim College of Business called “transformational,” reflects the growing presence of excess and surplus lines coverage in Florida, a state that in recent years saw many policyholders turn to surplus lines because of rising primary-market premiums and insurers’ litigation costs.
Surplus lines’ policy counts in Florida climbed from less than 1.2 million in 2020, for example, to more than 1.7 million in 2025. Total surplus lines’ premium in the state more than doubled, from $7.5 billion in 2020 to $17.3 billion in 2025, the FSLSO’s annual reports indicate.
The Surplus Lines Office, established by Florida statute in 1997, is a non-profit, quasi-governmental body that oversees compliance and collection of taxes on surplus lines policies, as well as an online portal for insurance agents and some back-office support for seven other states’ stamping offices.
The FSLSO appears to be well positioned to provide large grants: Last year, the organization reported almost $20 million in revenue from stamping fees and assessments on surplus policies. That’s more than double its revenue in 2020 and well above its reported 2025 expenses of $11.5 million. Total assets stood at almost $78 million, the annual report shows.
If anyone should question whether such revenue and margins are appropriate, the FSLSO’s director of communications pointed out that the office this year slashed its stamping fee in half, bringing it from .06% per policy to .03%. That’s less than $300 per policy and is the lowest among surplus lines stamping offices nationwide, FSLSO Communications Director Ashlee Weber noted.
The average surplus lines premium was about $7,700 in the third quarter of this year, the Office reported.
The $12 million endowment to FSU will establish the Florida Surplus Lines Center for Insurance Excellence and will be used to fund faculty salary stipends, student assistance, conferences and more.
“Our continued support, including this endowment, reflects our commitment to strengthening both the surplus lines industry and the broader insurance marketplace by investing in the education, research and talent that will shape the future,” Mark Shealy, FSLSO’s executive director, said in a statement.
Shealy graduated from FSU with a bachelor’s degree in accounting in 1991 before starting his career in the insurance industry.
The center will be led by FSU Professor Charles Nyce, who is already known for his department’s research into property-casualty insurance in recent years. Nyce’s position as director was funded by a separate, $1 million grant from the FSLSO that was announced in August.
Nyce said the center will be able to delve deeply into many areas of insurance, including property, liability and health insurance.

When Jane Kim claimed victory in the race for California insurance commissioner over fellow Democrat Ben Allen less than a week after the Nov. 3 election, the insurance industry may have gotten a more progressive and pro-consumer advocate than it has had in years.
Kim is a more progressive candidate than Allen, who was focused on making insurance affordable and fighting climate change in his work in the state Legislature.
Kim, an attorney and consumer advocate, served on San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors from 2011 to 2019. She has also run for state Senate and for San Francisco mayor. Her platform included providing natural disaster insurance for everyone, ensuring that premiums go to paying for claims, increasing transparency from insurers and investing in safer homes and communities.
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), for whom she served as California political director, the California Teachers Association and the Working Families Party all endorsed Kim.
Kim had 54.2% of the vote with all precincts reporting at least partially in. Vote-by-mail ballots, provisional ballots and other ballots are being tallied, but her lead has continued to grow to more than 900,000 votes over Allen.
She will replace outgoing commissioner Ricardo Lara, who is term limited.
Kim is also proposing a public program to cover wildfire risk for existing homes in California. In an October outline, she said participation would be mandatory, with premiums based partly on each home’s wildfire risk and partly on rebuilding costs to fund catastrophic losses. Private insurers would continue selling other homeowners coverages, and the public program would invest reserves in wildfire mitigation. The proposal would require support from state lawmakers and the governor.
Affordability was a recurring theme during her campaign, a message Democrats and progressives like her across the country rode to success in the elections.
“We’ve been traveling up and down the state all year and I just believe that our message centered around affordability and fighting to make sure that insurance is there for 40 million Americans in California resonated,” Kim said.

After canceling more than 6,600 flights on Saturday, airlines scrapped nearly 2,000 on Sunday, with more than 8,600 others being delayed, as of 7 p.m. New York time, according to data from tracker FlightAware.
American Airlines Group Inc. is showing the most canceled flights so far on Sunday, with 630, while JetBlue Airways Corp. has shed more than a quarter of its schedule.

“Those routers were purchased in 2001,” Duffy said on ABC’s This Week. “They were obsolete in 2006, and we still use them in 2026 just to underscore how old the network is.”

A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard identified the vessel as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance, which was built in 2013 and sails under the flag of Singapore.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down. The bridge reopened to traffic with a lane closure Thursday evening, the Burlington County (New Jersey) Bridge Commission Police Department said.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.
Associated Press journalists Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Julie Carr Smyth in Columbus, Ohio, and Christopher L. Keller in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed.

The U.S. Transportation Department wrongly decided to withhold nearly $74 million in highway money from New York state after it refused to revoke nearly 33,000 questionable commercial driver’s licenses for immigrants when an audit revealed problems last year, a federal appeals court said Friday.
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan concluded in a written decision that the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, an arm of the Transportation Department, acted in a manner that was “arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law” when it penalized New York.
The appeals court said the state can’t be faulted for failing to cancel licenses when a commercial driver lost legal status to stay in the United States because rules that would require a cancellation were not in place at the time.
The licenses pertain to commercial vehicles such as trucks, trailers, limousines and buses.
New York Attorney General Letitia James complained when the lawsuit was filed in April that the federal government was unfairly holding back money the state needs to repair roads and bridges. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring called the federal cuts “devastating” and characterized them as “political payback.”
The Transportation Department said in a statement Friday that it makes no sense for states to let trucking licenses for foreign drivers stretch years beyond when they are legally in the U.S.
“We’ve put a stop to the madness to keep the driving public safe,” the statement said.
Hochul and James welcomed the ruling in a joint statement, calling it “a win for the millions of New Yorkers who rely on safe roads to travel” and for the “drivers who power our state’s economy.”
The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers in the summer of 2025. Concerns about truck driver qualifications took on more urgency after an August 2025 crash in Florida, when a truck driver was accused of performing an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place.
Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant’s work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying citizenship status.
Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally.
Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers while the non-domiciled licenses immigrants can receive represent about 5% of all commercial driver’s licenses or about 200,000 drivers.
Immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted.
The dispute came after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy tightened rules governing when immigrants can obtain a commercial driver’s license.
Officials said they took action against states like New York after learning that some licenses remained valid long after an immigrant was no longer authorized to be in the country. New York issued licenses valid for eight years regardless of how long a driver’s visa remained valid, authorities said.
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska.

The California Department of Insurance is seeking information from insurers on their use of artificial intelligence as well as public input on potential safeguards covering transparency, accountability, privacy and fairness.
The CDI announced its Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Survey to examine how insurers are deploying AI technologies, the governance structures used to oversee those systems, the role of third-party vendors and operational impacts associated with AI adoption.
The department is also holding a virtual public workshop Dec. 15 beginning. Consumers, insurance companies, researchers, technology developers, academics, consumer advocates and other interested parties are invited to participate in the 10 a.m. workshop, which will focus on transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, accountability and insurer responsibility for technologies supplied by third-party vendors.
Information gathered through the survey and workshop will help the department determine whether additional consumer safeguards, transparency standards or regulatory guidance are needed, according to a CDI announcement about the survey and workshop.
The department plans to use the information collected to inform its AI oversight. Survey responses are due Dec. 30.

Adobe’s Sam Garfield: AI has Sped Up Creative, But Organizations Haven’t Kept Pace
RANCHO PALOS VERDES, CALIF. — Creative ideation that once took weeks now takes days, and sometimes hours. Versioning an asset across channels, formats, and aspect ratios has sped up just as much. The slowdown has moved somewhere else.
According to Sam Garfield, head of Digital Strategy, CMT, Data and AI Platforms at Adobe, the friction now sits inside the enterprise operating model. AI works well within individual functions, and companies struggle to roll it out across workflows.
“58% of the companies we talk to are in what we call the frozen middle,” Garfield told Beet.TV contributor David Kaplan at Beet Retreat LA, citing Adobe’s research on organizational readiness. “That means they’re stuck in their AI deployment, either in a pilot or not being able to deploy at scale.”
Moving to the left
Garfield describes the creative process as a content supply chain, and AI is changing how it starts. A creative brief used to be a document. Now it can kick off the generation of creative and the pulling of an audience in a single automated workflow.
One Adobe customer summed up the goal for her team in a phrase Garfield liked. She wanted them to “move to the left,” toward strategy at the start of the process and away from production at the end.
“What we’re doing is helping teams move to the left,” Garfield said.
One-stop agencies
Asked whether agency value is shifting toward strategy, audience insight, data stewardship, or orchestration, Garfield answered “all of the above.” Agencies are collapsing the silos that once separated creative, media, and activation, and clients increasingly expect a single integrated offering. Adobe, he said, is the operating system many agencies are building on top of.
Data that doesn’t connect
Audience data exists, and so does creative effectiveness data. Garfield sees the challenge in joining the two. A Winterberry Group study Garfield mentioned found that every company surveyed is measuring creative effectiveness or planning to, but only 6% use it at every point in the process.
“The data exists, but connecting the data and making sure that’s flowing back into which audience you select and then through the creative for effectiveness measurement is not happening at scale,” Garfield said.
Governance by design
Garfield argues that brand safety and rights compliance can’t be a gate at the end of the process when AI moves this quickly. Adobe has built those capabilities into its products, including brand intelligence checks such as whether a generated asset places the logo correctly.
“We don’t look at governance as something that happens at the end, as sort of a gate at the end. It has to be designed as part of the feature set,” Garfield said.

Microsoft (MSFT) stock trades at 27.3 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. At that price you want to know exactly what you own, and the company’s priorities have moved. During its fiscal Q2 2025 call in January 2025, management talked up customers such as UBS moving workloads to Azure, and it still made the case for cloud migrations a year later. On its October 2026 call, management emphasized something else. What does management talk up now instead?
Microsoft Now Talks Up Foundry And AI Agents
Management now emphasizes Foundry, the platform customers use to build AI agents and deploy them at scale, calling it an increasingly important driver of growth. On the October 28, 2026 call, management said Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, driven by Foundry and by earning more from its CPU capacity.
A cloud migration moves a customer’s existing work onto Azure, Microsoft’s cloud. On the fiscal Q4 2025 call in July 2025, management said Azure had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%.
Investors paying a premium for Microsoft appear to be betting that Azure can keep growing on new AI work rather than on workloads moved over from elsewhere. So far management has named Foundry as a driver of Azure’s growth in fiscal Q1 2027, though it said that growth also spanned core cloud services.
How Big Are Azure And Foundry Now?
Management said on the July 29, 2026 call that Azure passed $100 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, up 41%. Microsoft’s total revenue passed $331 billion that year, up 18%, so Azure grew more than twice as fast as the company.
That gap held in the latest quarter. Microsoft’s revenue rose 18.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, well short of Azure’s pace.
Foundry is growing faster still. Microsoft now has more than 120,000 Foundry customers, and management said Foundry revenue more than tripled from a year earlier. Foundry feeds a cloud business already worth more than $100 billion a year.
Is Microsoft’s New Focus Reassuring For Holders?
On growth, the shift looks reassuring. You also want to know what the data centers behind that growth cost. In fiscal Q1 2027, Microsoft’s cash from operations rose to $58.0 billion from $45.1 billion a year earlier. Yet as reported, fiscal Q1 2027 free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, fell to $18.6 billion from $25.7 billion a year earlier.
Management expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, against $45.2 billion in fiscal Q1. That measure counts finance leases in full when each lease starts. The cash Microsoft paid for property, plant and equipment in Q1 was $39.4 billion. Management’s guide for the full fiscal 2027 is that Microsoft will remain free cash flow positive, and management said it will tap additional sources of funding when it finds them attractive. At the end of September 2026, Microsoft held $64.3 billion of cash and short-term investments, more than its $57.2 billion of debt.
So Foundry is one named driver of Azure’s growth so far, while the cash that pays for the data centers is the weaker side. If free cash flow falls further, holders own a faster-growing Microsoft that keeps less of its sales as cash. Azure growth, against management’s guide of 49% to 50% in constant currency for fiscal Q2 2027, and free cash flow are the two numbers to watch when Microsoft reports in January 2027.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that accused the NCAA of misleading college sports fans by allowing transgender athletes to participate in events marketed as women’s competitions.
The lawsuit, filed in December 2024, said the NCAA falsely marketed events as women’s athletics in violation of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
“Radical ‘gender theory’ has no place in college sports,” Paxton said in a 2024 news release announcing the lawsuit.
The attorney general’s office Thursday informed the state district court in Lubbock that it will not proceed with the lawsuit. The court filing was first reported by Bloomberg Law.
In a statement after the lawsuit was filed, the NCAA did not address the allegations but said it would continue to support women’s sports.
The attorney general’s office and the NCAA did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.
Paxton’s office has dropped at least two other lawsuits since the Nov. 3 election when Paxton lost his bid for the U.S. Senate and Democrat Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton to become the next attorney general. Johnson has said he intends to review Paxton-era lawsuits and halt action on those deemed political in nature.
Last week, Paxton’s office dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down FIEL, a Houston immigrant-rights organization the state had accused of violating nonprofit restrictions by criticizing the immigration policies of President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Paxton’s office cited social media posts encouraging people to vote against Trump’s immigration proposals. The group opposed a 2023 Texas law that let Texas police arrest people suspected of having entered the country illegally.
The office also dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down Annunciation House, an El Paso migrant shelter that Paxton accused of illegally harboring undocumented immigrants.
“It’s very gratifying that this has now ended. It’s over,” Ruben Garcia, founder and executive director of Annunciation House, told El Paso Matters.
Republican messaging during the midterm elections was sharply focused on transgender people, particularly regarding youth and sports. It was also a topic that Johnson and Middleton frequently clashed over on the campaign trail and dates back to their days in the Texas senate together.

The Kentucky Department of Insurance has approved a recommendation that will keep average workers’ compensation loss costs unchanged—a rare non-decrease in an era that has seen annual reductions in most states for the last two decades.
The 0.0% change for the voluntary market will take effect Jan. 1, the DOI said in a bulletin. It follows a 9.7% average decrease for 2026 and similar cuts in preceding years.
The National Council on Compensation Insurance in September recommended keeping the course on average loss costs for 2027, based on loss experience in Kentucky from policy years 2022, 2023 and 2024.
“Policy year 2024 produced a higher loss ratio than observed in the prior two policy years. It is not yet clear whether the loss ratio increase in policy year 2024 can be attributed to year-over-year volatility or the start of a longer-term trend in Kentucky,” the NCCI wrote in a summary of its recommendations.
The year 2024 saw an increase in claim frequency, a deviation from a historical pattern of declines in frequency, the NCCI noted. Indemnity claim severity remained stable, while medical severity decreased that year.
Across the 38 states for which NCCI serves as a rating and analytics agency, the 2025 combined ratio for workers’ comp insurers rose, from 86% to 91%. After many years of declining worker injury rates across the country, the Council said the change in combined ratio is due primarily to an increase in loss and underwriting expense ratios.
Payroll also has increased around the country, putting upward pressure on premiums.
“From 2024 to 2025, payroll increased 4.8%, while employment rose just 0.5%,” the NCCI noted. A significant portion of payroll growth appears to have come from higher wages, which were up an average of 4.3% in 2025. Employment growth was largely driven by the health care sector.

New World screwworm spreading rapidly across Southern states
A pinned specimen of a full-grown New World screwworm fly is shown in this image. Federal and state officials are grappling with a worsening infestation from the flesh-eating parasite that threatens livestock, pets and wildlife. (Photo courtesy of Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife)
A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest.
Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three states. While fewer than 10 total cases were recorded in August and September, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has already confirmed 53 cases this month.
“We got a bunch more cases all of a sudden,” said David Anderson, professor and extension economist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University.
Rising infections have pushed state leaders to designate certain outbreak areas across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, where animal movement is being restricted.
The movement of pets and livestock is restricted in all or parts of 31 Texas counties as officials there are tracking 77 sites with at least one confirmed case.
Contrary to its name, the screwworm grows into an adult fly about the size of a common housefly. The name screwworm refers to the larvae (maggots) that burrow into open wounds, feeding as they go “like a screw being driven into wood,” according to USDA.
The pest could threaten beef and dairy cattle — potentially exacerbating high prices for consumers. But the screwworm can also infect people, wildlife and pets. That’s pushed states to recommend or require certain monitoring of pet movements.
California, for instance, requires all warm-blooded animals coming from an infested zone to have a pretravel inspection, a veterinary certification and an entry permit into the state. In Texas, adoptions for thousands of dogs and cats were put on hold in August as most states restricted movement of animals from areas with screwworm infestations.
“It’s thrown a wrench into things, for small rescues as well as the bigger shelters,” Mia Bendixsen, executive director of the Texas Humane Legislation Network, told The Associated Press.
Earlier this month, the New Mexico Livestock Board broadened its screwworm tracking to regional infestation zones as more cases were confirmed across southern parts of the state. Those zones demarcate where ranchers must receive state authorization before moving cattle.
“We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” New Mexico State Veterinarian Samantha Holeck said in an October statement, according to Source New Mexico.
Screwworm maggots burrow into the flesh of living animals through wounds as small as a tick bite or in body openings such as the eyes or nose. That means ranchers must keep close watch over newborn calves with exposed umbilical cords and may need to rethink branding and tagging operations that provide an entry for the pests.
While the flies could prove deadly to herds, USDA says they do not create food safety risks.
But a worsening infestation could impact beef prices, which are already near record high prices.

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.
Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.
Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, says Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
Keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try new fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”
If you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?
Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

How Much Runners Can Reduce Mileage to Maintain Fitness
First, it’s important to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.
“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” says Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.
Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy says. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.
This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy says.

Most runners are familiar with the big muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.
A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.
When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.
If this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew says. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.
What Causes QL Pain?
There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a big, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.
Another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.
Yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can issues in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas says.
Keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas says. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”
How Does a Tight QL Affect Running?
A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great issues if left unchecked. A big one? Compromised running mechanics.
A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew says. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

TORONTO, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As organizations work to turn AI initiatives into measurable results at scale, a new global study from the IBM Institute for Business Value (IBV) finds that Chief AI Officers are positioned to see where AI is delivering value or falling short across the enterprise, but few fully control the decisions needed to act on those insights. In Canada, the findings point to a gap between the urgency organizations place on AI transformation and their ability to turn AI strategy into action.
Based on a global survey of 1,667 Chief AI Officers (CAIOs) and equivalent senior AI leaders across 33 geographies, the study found that only 18% have full control over AI investment decisions. Nearly half (48%) say AI agents already initiate and execute actions across workflows, yet 75% report that governance, risk or compliance considerations delay AI-driven action.
Canadian AI leaders face an execution gap as organizations race to transform with AI
According to the study, three-quarters (75%) of Canadian senior AI leaders surveyed believe their organizations risk falling behind competitors in AI transformation if they continue at their current pace. Yet only 15% have full authority over AI investment decisions.
The gap extends beyond decision rights. Seventy per cent of Canadian respondents say their organizations do not quickly adjust decisions and resources when AI performance measurement identifies opportunities to improve outcomes. The findings also underscore the need to balance between AI autonomy and governance: 42% say AI agents already initiate and execute actions autonomously across workflows, while 73% say governance, risk or compliance considerations delay AI-driven action.
"The AI conversation in Canada is shifting from experimentation to execution. Canadian organizations understand the need to move quickly, but successful pilots alone will not deliver transformation. Organizations need to connect AI strategy, investment decisions and workflow redesign so they can turn AI insights into measurable business outcomes at scale," said Matthew Wetmore, Consulting Managing Partner & Market Leader, IBM Canada.

What Are Apple Investors Betting On?
Today’s big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash
Apple (AAPL) stock trades at 36.0 times its earnings over the last twelve months, counted as normalized net income plus stock-based pay after tax, with the shares near their highest close of the past year. That is a high price for one year of profit, so it is worth setting against the profit expected over the next two fiscal years. So what sales and profit does that price assume Apple will deliver?
Apple Investors Bet On Higher Sales At Thinner Margins
The consensus forecast projects Apple’s revenue will reach $528 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with the $479 billion reported for fiscal 2026. Forecasted net income rises far less, moving to $135 billion from $132 billion. Those figures leave a net margin of 25.6% in fiscal 2027, below the 27.6% Apple reported for fiscal 2026.
For fiscal 2028, the forecast models a 7.4% increase in revenue and a 10.3% rise in net income. That puts the net margin at 26.3%, still short of fiscal 2026. The bet is on more sales, not on more profit from each dollar of sales.
On that forecast, you pay 38.0 times the average analyst estimate of Apple’s net income for fiscal 2027. That is not measured the same way as the 36.0 times trailing figure, which adds stock-based pay after tax to normalized net income. On fiscal 2028 earnings the price is 34.4 times, though that year’s forecast is uncertain: the gap between the highest and lowest per-share estimates is 23.8% of the average.
How Fast Has Apple Actually Been Growing?
Apple’s latest year ran faster than the forecast: revenue increased 15.1% in fiscal 2026, after 6.4% growth in fiscal 2025. The consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 works out to about 10% growth. Neither forecasted margin surpasses what the company has already reached: Apple reported a net margin of 26.9% in fiscal 2025 and posted a higher margin in fiscal 2026.
The iPhone led that growth, with sales rising 21.2% in fiscal 2026. Services, Apple’s second-largest business, grew 13.0%.
Management guidance points to a slower start for fiscal 2027. Apple expects December quarter revenue to grow 7% to 10%. Management said this range reflects constrained supply, noting that revenue grew 16% in the same quarter a year before. The company also expects a gross margin of 45% to 46%. Management said most of the margin decline from the September quarter comes from higher memory costs.
Where Could Apple Fall Short Of The Forecast?
Supply is the first place. Management expects memory to constrain the Mac and iPad in the December quarter because demand has been higher than it expected. Apple provides no outlook beyond that quarter. If those constraints last, the fiscal 2027 sales forecast could come down.
The cost of memory is the other place. Beyond the December quarter, management sees memory prices still rising and expects less help over time from memory already in inventory. Price increases on the Mac, iPad and iPhone have offset some of that impact, but further cost rises could push Apple’s net margin below the forecast.
If the forecast holds, the forward multiples are a fair picture of Apple’s price. Supply is where the forecast is most likely to fall short, and lower sales alongside rising memory costs would leave the stock priced for profit Apple may never earn, a riskier bet. When school boards offer members of the public the opportunity to speak at their meetings, they generally impose limits on time, subject matter and the number of speakers who can participate in a given meeting. Many districts, including Raytown, require that public comments be related to items already on the board meeting agenda.

Only 18% of surveyed CAIOs have full control over AI investment decisions
Only 29% say their organizations quickly adjust decisions and resources when AI performance insights reveal opportunities to improve results
Nearly half say AI agents act across workflows, yet 75% report that governance, risk, or compliance delays AI-driven action
ARMONK, N.Y., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As companies struggle to convert AI initiatives into measurable results at scale, a new IBM (NYSE: IBM) Institute for Business Value study suggests that Chief AI Officers are well positioned to see where the technology is creating value or falling short across the enterprise -- yet few control the decisions needed to act on those insights.
The global study*, based on a survey of more than 1,600 Chief AI Officers (CAIOs) and equivalent enterprise AI leaders, reveals that only 18% of respondents say they have full control over AI investment decisions.
That disconnect is reflected in how organizations redesign the business and make resource decisions. Fewer than one-third of surveyed CAIOs say AI is reshaping the business model, including what the organization sells, how it prices, or how it captures value. Just 29% of respondents say their organizations adjust decisions and resources quickly when AI performance insights identify opportunities to improve outcomes.
Joanne Wright, Senior Vice President, Transformation and Operations at IBM, writes in the study's foreword: "Few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise. Yet the outcomes they [Chief AI Officers] are accountable for often depend on decisions made by others. This means successful AI leadership requires more than technical expertise or operational oversight. It requires gathering evidence, influencing decisions, and measuring success."
The study identifies a group of high-impact CAIOs whose organizations report stronger results. These leaders report that 63% of AI projects deliver measurable business outcomes, compared with 43% for all other CAIOs, and that 49% move from pilot to production, versus 33%. They also scale successful initiatives enterprise-wide in eight months, compared with 13.5 months among all other CAIOs. The findings link these stronger outcomes with differences in how the organizations manage AI autonomy and control, redesign business workflows, and make evidence-based investment decisions.
Other study findings include:
CAIOs balance greater AI autonomy with stronger control
48% of CAIOs say AI agents initiate and execute actions across workflows, yet 75% say governance, risk or compliance delays AI-driven action.
While 73% of respondents have defined where human oversight is non-negotiable, only 61% say AI decision rights are clearly defined and consistently applied.
High-impact CAIOs are nearly four times as likely to say they can quickly pause, adjust or redirect AI systems without disrupting operations.
At the same time, 96% of high-impact CAIOs say AI-generated outputs can trigger actions autonomously, compared with 40% of all other CAIOs.
Organizations are scaling AI faster than redesigning the business around it
While only 32% say AI is reshaping the business model, 35% of CAIOs say it primarily strengthens the existing model, and 26% expect it to reshape the model but have not made the necessary shifts.
71% of CAIOs believe their organizations risk falling behind competitors in AI transformation.

New Zealand’s central bank warned on Tuesday that global financial stability risks continue to rise, with growing vulnerabilities in the non-bank lending sector driven by increased private credit activity.
In its semi-annual Financial Stability Report, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) said non-bank lenders are becoming more active in the country, particularly in commercial property and development financing.
While greater competition offers benefits for borrowers, it creates risks that are harder for the RBNZ to monitor, as much of this activity falls outside the regulated sector, it said.
Read more: Private Credit and Stablecoins Pose Risks Beyond Size, BoE Governor Bailey Warns
“While systemic risks from non-bank lenders in New Zealand remain limited given their size, their growing role in credit provision highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring,” the report said.
Banks continue to account for the majority of lending to households and businesses in New Zealand, with direct finance and non-bank lending firms representing only about 6% of overall lending, official data showed. Private credit funds and non-bank lenders are not directly regulated by the RBNZ, which also serves as the country’s banking regulator.
The RBNZ highlighted how the recent failure of an Australian property developer exposed several private lenders to potential losses, with some funds restricting withdrawals amid increased redemption requests.
Last week, Australia’s corporate regulator said it would launch an official probe into the A$3.4 billion ($2.30 billion) collapse of Sydney homebuilder Bathla, putting fresh scrutiny on the fast-growing private credit sector, which has increasingly stepped in to finance developers as banks retreat from riskier lending.
The financial stability report also warned that heightened geopolitical tensions and financial market fragility had increased global risks, with Middle East tensions disrupting energy and trade flows.
However, the report said New Zealand’s financial system remained resilient.
“Domestic financial stress has generally eased from its peak last year but remains uneven,” RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said.
Despite some narrowing of lending margins, New Zealand’s banks are maintaining strong capital and liquidity positions, with recent stress tests showing banks and insurers could withstand severe financial shocks, Breman added.

The defunding of weather observation systems across the world as countries focus on military spending is making it harder to predict extreme events at a time when the planet is reaching unprecedented heat levels.
Weather and climate observations worth about $10 billion globally are at risk, according to the World Meteorological Organization. Key measurements have already declined and others could be interrupted, said the WMO’s Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, in an interview on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. (Editor’s note: This article was published by Bloomberg on Nov. 11).
“Geopolitical tensions have resulted in a large majority of governments redirecting their investments to defense, instead of observing and understanding the climate system and preparing to adapt to it,” Saulo said. In terms of observations, she added, “We are increasingly far from solving a problem that’s not hard to solve.”
Data gathered in hundreds of weather stations across the world are essential to allow forecasters to make predictions on storms, heat waves and drought. They also feed into early-warning systems that can alert populations just before disasters strike. In addition, scientific models depend on that information to make long-term projections of how man-made global warming will impact the planet.
Because climate investment from developed countries is falling, “everything points to a decline in adaptation funding in 2026 and 2027 that will have a great impact on observation systems,” Saulo said. “Many countries in the Global South have no resources to invest.”
The risk that the US will defund global ocean observations is of particular concern, she said, because no other country has the capacity to deploy resources to gather ocean data at a similar scale. A halt in these observations would lead to a so-called single point of failure, in which the ocean observations system collapses.
“Everyone assumes the system will keep functioning as it has for the past 20 years, but that’s not the case,” she said. “When the system stops working, it will be too late.”
The WMO Global Climate Observing System, which assesses the state of global climate observations, needs $500 million a year to operate, while coordination efforts with different agencies cost about $10 million a year. Developing nations need a combined $150 million a year to strengthen their observation systems, the WMO estimates. All of that is under threat, Saulo said.
“These are not unimaginable sums,” she added. However, “private sectors and philanthropists are not assuming that responsibility either.”
Lack of funding is an issue across the whole UN climate system. The UN Framework Convention for Climate Change has warned it needs more money to facilitate increasingly large events like COP31 and to provide the growing amount of reports countries are asking for.

Japan will create a network across the Asia-Pacific region to promote development of early-warning systems aimed at bolstering protections against extreme weather events and natural disasters.
Gaps in capabilities such as remote sensing and cellphone alerts have been highlighted by recent events, including the devastating August floods near the Nepal-China border, which killed more than 1,400 people and wiped out towns, border posts and hydropower plants
“The network will share knowledge and expertise in the introduction and operation of the early warning systems and promote effective deployment,” Japan’s Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa said Tuesday in a speech to the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkey.
Japan, which lies on an arc of volcanoes and fault lines surrounding the Pacific Basin known as the “Ring of Fire,” has been a pioneer in earthquake early-warning systems and developing buildings designed to withstand powerful tremors.
The country also remains committed to supporting countries with climate finance, though sees a need for other nations to contribute more, Sasagawa said.
“To meet the needs of countries requiring support, it is essential to broaden the contributor base to include countries capable of contributing, and to expand various financial flows including private finance,” he said at the conference.
Developed economies have persistently called for the likes of China, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states to expand their climate finance contributions, while those nations argue that most responsibility should rest with countries that industrialized first.

[Editor’s Note: This Community Voices article was written by Daan Oxener, who is a Dutch entrepreneur and tennis player who somewhat accidentally found his way into Kapchorwa’s running culture. Since 2016, he has explored Mount Elgon’s many trails and everyday community life. Through Home of Friends Guesthouse and Run Kapchorwa, he helps adventurous travelers discover the people and stories behind Uganda’s Land of Champions.]
The moment you climb the tarmac road to Kapchorwa, Uganda, you are surrounded by rolling green hills, banana plantations, and small farms. There is little sign that you are approaching one of East Africa’s elite running hubs. Kapchorwa’s first impression is rural and rustic. No tartan running tracks or fancy facilities here.
Alvin, an ambitious U.K. runner with Ugandan roots, describes his first experience of running on Kapchorwa’s trails:
‘‘The trails are very scenic. You cross small villages and rivers. The trail surfaces are made of mud with small rocks, but they are quite smooth. You see a lot of farm life. You come across the locals, children walking to school. Nothing extravagant.’’
But in this unassuming environment, international athletes are pushing their limits. And so did Alvin.
‘‘Because of my excitement to find elite athletes, I pushed myself more than I should have. I was struggling to keep pace with a group of local runners. Later I was told that Jacob Kiplimo, the world half marathon and cross-country champion, was in this group.’’
Running in Kapchorwa is challenging and takes time to adapt to. We see this with almost every international runner who comes here for the first time. The rule, therefore, is simple: Change the altitude, but leave everything else the same.
Compared with the famous running hub of Iten, Kenya, its counterpart across the border, Kapchorwa is greener and hillier. The two places share ancestral Kalenjin roots, reflected in similarities in culture and food. In terms of infrastructure, however, they are quite different: Iten has more tarmac roads, and its running tourism infrastructure is more developed, with gyms and swimming pools catering to visiting athletes.
The Mount Elgon Rainforest
‘‘Give us the forest back, and we give Uganda more champions.’’
This recurring message from elders in the Mosopisiek community says a lot about the roots of Kapchorwa’s running culture.
In 1992, when the Ugandan portion of Mount Elgon National Park was officially gazetted, many Mosopisiek people were relocated from the rainforest to the lower flanks of the mountain.
This meant a big change in their way of life: from running for miles after stolen cows to settling in one area and growing potatoes or onions; from eating forest berries and mushrooms to eating grains and plantains.
But those roots have not disappeared. You can still experience them on trail runs and hikes through the stunning, undulating landscape.
Daily endurance, or “building stamina” as the natives often describe it, starts from a young age. Children walk kilometers to school. In their free time, they jump over steep rocks and mountain streams.
The terrain itself is a training ground.
The lifestyle of today’s runners is still closely intertwined with life in and around the forest. Runners know: If I want to be prepared for the next race, I need to take natural honey from the forest. Or I need to train on the steep paths leading up to 3,000 meters above sea level.
